newsitem.title: FRANCE: Boissonnat sees no changes from new BoF members.
newsitem.headline: Boissonnat sees no changes from new BoF members.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac's appointment of two new members to the Bank of France's monetary policy council does not signify any change in policy, outgoing member Jean Boissonnat said in a magazine interview.

"He perhaps had a desire for influence in naming people close to him, but it remains at the level of form," Boissonnat said in the interview to be published in Thursday's edition of weekly L'Expansion.
"The President is too committed to revise his European policy," Boissonnat said.

Economists had suggested that the appointment by the government last week of Pierre Guillen and Jean-Rene Bernard to the Bank's nine-member monetary policy council might soften its hard line in defending the stability of the franc against the mark.

For France, the franc-mark link is the cornerstone to the future European single currency and any softening in its commitment to currency stability would be seen as a weakening in its commitment to European monetary union.

Boissonnat, who was viewed as a staunch supporter of the Bank's hawkish governor, Jean-Claude Trichet, said it would be wrong to assume the appointment of the new members would create a new balance of power in the council.
The appointments have been seen as potentially creating a five-to-four majority in favour of faster interest rate cuts, overturning a previous six-to-three majority backing Trichet.
Boissonnat said there had never been any systematic majority at the council, "but a majority which varied according to the decisions to be taken".

He also said the government must work harder to explain the benefits of monetary union to the public. "My worry, and it is real, is that the single currency, once created, explodes at take-off," he said.
But he said that he remained convinced the single currency would be launched on schedule in January, 1999.
